findings.input: new ForeignTokenRegistry([{ name: "acme", pattern: /ACME_[A-Z0-9_]+/g }]).namespaceOf("ACME_ABCDEF_0001") called repeatedly
findings.config: foreign registry with a pattern-registered namespace whose RegExp carries the g (or y) flag
findings.expected_invariant: The same registration must yield the same ownership verdict on every call, and classifyOwnership / ctx.isProtectedToken / the forward path must agree with each other. Registry contract: a registered foreign token is PRESERVED on the input path.
findings.observed: namespaceOf alternates acme/null/acme/null because RegExp.prototype.test on a g or y matcher advances lastIndex; classifyOwnership resets lastIndex before matching while isProtectedToken does not, so the two layers fight over one matcher object. Consequence: DB_PASSWORD=ACME_ABCDEF_0001 is redacted to DB_PASSWORD=CRG_... instead of being preserved, and the verdict depends on call order.
findings.impact: ownership/policy inconsistency + deployment correctness. A shared registry built once at startup gives different results than one built per request. No confidentiality leak: the failure direction is over-redaction. An EXACT registration is unaffected.
findings.control: an equivalent non-stateful matcher (/ACME_[A-Z0-9_]+/) preserves the token correctly, which locates the defect in how the matcher is used rather than in the registry's purpose
findings.root_cause: normalizeForeignNamespace kept the caller's RegExp object unchanged and namespaceOf called .test() directly. On a g or y matcher .test() advances lastIndex, so the same token alternated between FOREIGN_REGISTERED and UNKNOWN; classifyOwnership reset lastIndex before matching while isProtectedToken did not, so the two layers fought over one shared matcher object and the verdict depended on call order.
findings.fix: Two layers. (1) normalizeForeignNamespace clones: new RegExp(pattern.source, pattern.flags), so neither side can observe the other's cursor. (2) A single namespaceMatches(matcher, value) helper resets lastIndex to 0 before the call and fixes it back to 0 in a finally block; namespaceFindAll does the same for the three String.match enumeration sites. Deliberately not 'save and restore the old value': a registry-internal matcher should not carry observable cursor state at all, so 0 is the honest end state.
findings.regression: test/adversarial/registry.test.js -- 100-call stability, cross-layer agreement, forward-path preservation, call-order independence (A,B,A,B,A vs A,A,A,B,B), caller-regex isolation in both directions, reusable-registry stability, exact-registration immunity, and every matcher shape.

findings.input: registry with { name: "acme", pattern: /ACME_[A-Z0-9_]+/y }; applySinkPolicy("curl x?y=ACME_ABCDEF_0001", ctx, { kind: "tool_argument" })
findings.config: foreign registry whose namespace matcher carries the sticky flag y
findings.expected_invariant: Ownership recognition must not depend on WHERE in a document a token appears. A registered foreign token that is protected in prose must also be protected as an operand, or the two channels disagree for one registration.
findings.observed: A sticky matcher only matches at lastIndex 0. namespaceOf calls .test() with the cursor at 0, and namespaceFindAll uses String.match which with y is anchored at lastIndex as well, so the registry cannot FIND a token that has anything before it. Result for one registration: namespaceOf("ACME_ABCDEF_0001") = acme and isProtectedToken = true, while inside "curl x?y=ACME_ABCDEF_0001" namespaceOf = null and an untrusted tool operand is DELIVERED instead of refused.
findings.impact: ownership/policy inconsistency between the prose channel and the operand channel for sticky registrations. No plaintext is exposed: the failure direction is that this layer hands over a token it cannot resolve, which the outer DLP owns. Severity Low, and only reachable with a sticky matcher, which the design does not recommend but does accept.
findings.reproduce: node --test test/adversarial/registry.test.js (test 'R2-REG OBSERVATION: a STICKY matcher cannot find a token mid-document')
findings.control: the equivalent /g matcher refuses the operand, which is the expected behaviour
findings.relationship: INDEPENDENT of R2-REG-001. Verified by stashing the stateful-matcher fix and re-running: the behaviour above is identical before and after, so it is pre-existing and was neither caused nor cured by that fix. Deliberately NOT folded into R2-REG-001, per the rule that several red points are usually not one root cause.
findings.fix: namespaceFindAll is now a real DOCUMENT SEARCH while namespaceOf keeps the matcher's declared semantics unchanged. The scan runs on a clone with y removed and g ensured, and every candidate it proposes is re-checked against the ORIGINAL matcher, so discovery is not authority and the registry's own matcher is never permanently rewritten. namespaceOf(TOKEN) = acme and namespaceOf(prefix + TOKEN) = null are both unchanged for a sticky matcher.
findings.regression: test/adversarial/registry.test.js -- membership unchanged in both directions for sticky; the operand is now refused; prose still preserves; the registry keeps its declared flags; every flag combination scans AND keeps its membership semantics (only y/gy are anchored, corrected from an earlier table that wrongly expected gi to be anchored); and admission is not widened, asserted on classifyOwnership rather than on a span, with a case-sensitivity control.

findings.input:
A=cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM0NTY3OA==   (minimal)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
data:
  a: cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM0NTY3OA==
  b: cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM0NTY3OA==   (K8s path)
findings.expected_invariant: The replacement is self-delimiting: a redaction replaces a whole value and leaves NO characters of the original beside it. R1 already pins that every emitted token matches ^CRG_[A-Z0-9]{4,}_[A-Z0-9]{4,}$ and that no truncated PREFIX survives; the converse -- a complete replacement with leftover characters glued to it -- is the uncovered half.
findings.observed: The entropy detector's span stops before base64 padding, so the padding survives next to the replacement. Minimal: `A=cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM0NTY3OA==` becomes `A=CRG_AAAAAA_0001==`, and the single-padding form becomes `A=CRG_AAAAAA_0001=`. In a K8s Secret the two occurrences of one plaintext produce two spans that differ by the padding -- gitleaks takes the padded form, entropy the unpadded one -- which overlap WITHOUT containment, so the merge keeps both and the second yields `b: Q1JHX0FBQUFBQV8wMDAy==`, a base64 encode of a second token with the ORIGINAL padding appended. Two occurrences of one plaintext therefore get two different replacements.
findings.impact: Integrity and representation correctness, in every context rather than only K8s: the emitted value is neither the replacement nor the original, `CRG_AAAAAA_0001==` is not a token and is not valid base64 either, and one plaintext acquires two identities. Round-trip happens to survive because the residual `==` is still the original's padding and restoration is substring-based -- asserted, so the claim is exact. No confidentiality fail-open was found.
findings.verified_pre_existing: Confirmed with `git stash` that the behaviour is identical with and without the R2-REG-001/R2-REG-002 fixes, so it is not related to those.
findings.why_r1_missed_it: R1's token-shape property removes every full token and then checks that no `CRG_` PREFIX remains. Residue that sits AFTER a complete token is invisible to that check, so the property only covered truncation, not trailing leftovers.
findings.root_cause: tokenizeBlocks() scores runs of [A-Za-z0-9]+ for entropy, so the EVIDENCE for a base64 scalar covers the core and stops before the padding. The consequence was 'one plaintext, two identities', but that is NOT a ledger defect: the raw strings handed to the mapping genuinely differed (occurrence 1 raw = padded form, occurrence 2 raw = unpadded form), so rawToToken legitimately allocated two identities. The chain is: entropy boundary truncation -> original representation residue survives -> the second occurrence's raw differs -> the mapping allocates a second identity, exactly as its contract says. The real defect is that detector evidence boundary != representation mutation boundary: the detector had already shown the core was worth protecting, but nothing treated the trailing `=` as part of the ENCODED SCALAR.
findings.fix: A narrow base64 REPRESENTATION envelope, alongside the existing reference and infra envelopes: the detector keeps the verdict, the representation supplies the boundary. base64ScalarAt() widens an evidence span by at most the padding bytes and only when the result is a complete canonical base64 scalar that STARTS where the span starts, ends at the scalar's end, has at most two padding characters, and decodes to printable text. classifiedText keeps the original detector core, so widening does not change the classification input -- the same rule the reference envelope follows. Deliberately NOT done: extending the entropy alphabet to include `=` (that pollutes the scoring model to solve a representation problem and moves every score), and a merge special case for entropy+gitleaks overlap (that would teach the geometry layer to parse base64 syntax).
findings.regression: test/adversarial/representation.test.js -- the emitted VALUE (extracted as the RHS, since the assignment's own `=` makes a whole-line search meaningless) must be exactly one complete token; every occurrence's boundary must cover the full encoded scalar; a K8s value must be canonical base64 AND ledger-owned AND resolve to an owned token; the same raw must no longer split into two identities; classification input stays the detector core; the matrix over env/yaml/k8s x H/G/H+G x no-padding/one-=/two-==; three occurrences sharing one identity. Negative controls: an `==` operator after a high-entropy run is not swallowed; a non-canonical, mis-positioned, over-padded or alphabet-continued candidate is not widened; and a canonical scalar IS widened, so the controls are not vacuous.
findings.oracle_corrections: Two regression oracles were wrong before the fix and were corrected first. (1) `out.includes(residue)` can never pass for residue '=' because the assignment itself contains '='; the value is now extracted and asserted to be a complete token. For the non-canonical single-'=' input the honest outcome is the token followed by the stray character, which is asserted explicitly. (2) The old test pinned the bug's shape with `assert.deepEqual(covered, [B64, B64.slice(0, -2)])`, which would fail the moment the implementation became correct; it now asserts the contract that each boundary covers the complete encoded scalar. Also measured: with `G only` the gitleaks rule does not fire on this blob because it gates on its own entropy check, so 'no padding survives' only applies once something was actually redacted.

findings.expected_invariant: Cost must scale with the number of candidates, not with candidates x document length. A span-density increase should stay near linear in the number of spans.
findings.observed: Doubling m multiplied the runtime by ~3.9 at every step up to m=1600 (disjoint 14/53/213/832/3321 ms, nested reaching 4.8 s at m=800). Instrumented call counting located it precisely: enclosingReference() was called once per span and re-scanned the WHOLE document each time, so the envelope phase was O(spans x text) -- at 800 spans it walked 12.7M bytes. The containment merge is separately O(m^2) (320k overlap comparisons at m=800) and runs twice per call, but measured as the smaller term.
findings.impact: Availability / DoS. A modest payload of ~23 KB with 800 hits took 832 ms of CPU and nested shapes 4.8 s, so a few hundred KB of candidate-dense input could occupy a worker for a long time. maxRedactions does NOT defend this stage: it fires during token minting, after candidate merge has already run.
findings.root_cause: The reference-envelope widening called enclosingReference(text, start, end) per span, and that helper recomputes referenceEnvelopes(text) -- a full scan of the document -- on every call. The result depends only on the document, so it was pure repeated work.
findings.fix: Compute the document's reference constructs ONCE per findSensitiveSpans call and answer every span's lookup by scanning that small set, keeping the same selection rule (narrowest strictly-containing construct, widened to the outermost). Measured at m=800: disjoint 832ms -> 27.8ms, nested 4816ms -> 41.0ms. Doubling ratios fell from ~3.9 to 2.1-3.0. All 400 tests pass unchanged, including the R2.4 attribution test.
findings.regression: test/r3-span-density.perf.test.js -- four shapes, sizes 100-800, median of 3 after a warmup, asserting that every tail doubling ratio stays under 3.2; a full-redaction variant so the minting stage cannot add its own superlinear term; and a printed scaling report. The heavy sizes, MB corpora and soak live in scripts/perf.mjs behind `npm run perf`.
findings.rejected_attempt: A first attempt also linearised the containment merge by sorting widest-first and scanning once with a running maximum end. That is NOT equivalent to the pairwise `some()` predicate: it moved attribution from gitleaks to entropy (caught by the R2.4 attribution test) and then broke 11 further tests in different ways. It was reverted in full, leaving only the envelope fix. The merge remains O(m^2), measured as a second-order term (m=3200: 178ms with it, 153ms without, i.e. ~15-35%), and is recorded as a watch item rather than silently rewritten.
findings.measurement_note: A single slow run is not a finding. The corpus is deterministic, timings are medians of 3 after a warmup, and the assertion requires EVERY tail ratio to exceed the bound rather than failing on one noisy sample. Absolute milliseconds are recorded but never asserted.

findings.input: 'x'.repeat(n) with flags {email: true}  -- a body containing no email at all
findings.config: findSensitiveSpans / RedactionContext.redactText with the email detector enabled; any n up to the 16 MiB body limit
findings.expected_invariant: Cost must be linear in the input length. A regex with no nested quantifier should not be able to consume superlinear time on input that does not match it.
findings.observed: The email detector's single unanchored pattern is quadratic on text containing no `@`. Measured end to end: 37ms at 4 KB, 126ms at 8 KB, 507ms at 16 KB, 2028ms at 32 KB, with the doubling ratio holding at ~4. Extrapolated: ~32s at 128 KB and ~34 minutes at 1 MiB, from a payload that contains no email. The regex has NO nested quantifier, which is why it survived review: the leading `[class]+` and the `@` are ambiguous, so at every start position the engine consumes the rest of the run and then fails on `@`.
findings.impact: Availability / DoS. Triggerable with ordinary text of a few hundred KB, well inside the default 16 MiB body limit, and no special characters or structure are required. Isolated to one detector: email-only cost equals all-flags cost, so it is not an interaction.
findings.root_cause: Ambiguous unanchored pattern rather than a nested quantifier. `collectRegexSpans(text, /[local]+@[domain]/g, ...)` gives the engine O(n) possible start positions, and at each one it scans to the end of the run before failing.
findings.fix: collectEmailSpans() locates `@` with indexOf -- the only positions where a match can start -- walks left over the local class, and matches the domain with an ANCHORED pattern against the remainder. Cost is linear in the number of `@` characters and a single scan when there are none. Measured: 131072 bytes of `x` went from ~32128ms (extrapolated from the pre-fix curve) to 9.54ms, and the email-only path now measures 1.36/2.43/9.54ms at 16K/32K/128K, i.e. linear. The accepted language is unchanged: character classes, the 63-character label limit and the required dot are all preserved, and the new implementation was compared against the old pattern on a 16-case fixture set with zero differences.
findings.regression: scripts/perf-redos.mjs family D-email-failing-tail, plus the existing email tests. The pathological form needs a bounded reproducer in the ordinary suite; the full geometric sweep stays behind `npm run perf:redos`.
findings.measurement_note: Adversarial/control ratio grew 2.74 -> 5.50 -> 12.29 -> 20.08 -> 42.19 across n=512..8192 while the tail exponent held near 1.75, which is the signature the R3 standard asks for: the ratio AMPLIFIES with n rather than settling, so it is backtracking and not ordinary scan cost. Both inputs in that family exercise the email pattern, which is why the control grew too.

findings.config: referenceEnvelopes() directly, or findSensitiveSpans / redactText with any flag set; the scanner runs on every document
findings.expected_invariant: Scanning a document for reference constructs is a single left-to-right pass over the text, so cost must be linear in the length. An UNCLOSED opener is ordinary text and should cost nothing beyond the scan.
findings.observed: The balanced scan runs from each opener to the end of the text when the construct never closes, and it does so once per opener-like position, so cost is O(n * openers). Measured on referenceEnvelopes() alone: 25.7ms at 2 KB, 302ms at 8 KB, 1212ms at 16 KB, 3813ms at 32 KB, with the doubling exponent holding at ~2.0. In the sweep this showed as adversarial/control ratios AMPLIFYING with n -- 12.05 -> 35.26 -> 86.36, and 9.97 -> 23.60 -> 48.14 -- which is the signature that distinguishes it from ordinary scan cost.
findings.impact: Availability / DoS. A few tens of KB of unclosed openers costs seconds of CPU, and the scanner runs on every request regardless of flags, so it is not gated behind a detector being enabled. Extrapolated to the default 16 MiB body limit the cost is hours.
findings.root_cause: In referenceEnvelopes(), when the balanced scan fails to find a closer it leaves `end` unset and advances i by one, so the next opener-like position repeats a scan that already ran to the end of the text. There is no memoisation of a failed scan, because the naive form of that memo is WRONG: a failed scan from i does not imply that positions inside it fail. `{{x}` is the counter-example -- scanning from 0 as a `{{` opener fails, but position 1 is a valid single-brace `{x}` construct that the current implementation finds.
findings.rejected_attempt: A prototype that marked the whole scanned range as failed changed the result on 19 of 22621 exhaustively generated strings of length 0..4 over a 12-character alphabet (`{{x}`, `{{_}`, `{$()`, `{%x%`, `{%_%`, `{<x>` -- all cases where an OUTER opener fails and an INNER opener succeeds). It was discarded rather than shipped, which is why the sweep still shows this as open.
findings.next_step: A correct fix has to keep per-position results while sharing the failure information. Two candidates: (a) scan once and record, for every position, the index where a balanced scan from there stops, then reuse those stops -- which is linear because the stop indices are monotone; (b) restructure to a single stack-based pass that emits constructs as it closes them, which is the conventional way to parse nested delimiters in one pass. Both need the exhaustive equivalence check above as the acceptance gate.
findings.regression: scripts/perf-redos.mjs families C-reference-unclosed, C-reference-depth and C-reference-siblings, all reporting amplifying adversarial/control ratios. No bounded reproducer is in the ordinary suite yet, because the fix is not in.
findings.found_via: The sweep's per-family summary. Note that three OTHER families that appeared as TIMEOUT in the pre-fix sweep (A-assignment-quote, A-assignment-separators, B-provider-wrong-tail) were NOT regex problems at all: their adversarial/control ratio was 1.00-1.07, i.e. both sides were equally slow because of the email detector. After the email fix they measure 24ms, 19ms and 37ms at 131072 bytes with linear exponents. That is exactly why a same-length control is required -- without it, a shared quadratic term reads as a regex finding.

algorithm_search.status: NOT RESOLVED. Five formulations attempted; none reached equivalence, and none was shipped. The finding stays open.
algorithm_search.oracle: The current referenceEnvelopes() is used as an oracle and compared by EXACT ARRAY (start, end, opener, order), never by count. Exhaustive over every string of length 0..5 on the 10-character alphabet { } $ ( ) % < > x _ = 111111 strings, plus targeted counterexamples.

attempts.idea: Predicate on prefix reachability per position with a per-family owed.
attempts.outcome: rejected by reasoning: computing the predicate needs the closure relation itself

attempts.idea: Predecessor-chain jump tables plus a failure memo.
attempts.outcome: REJECTED. Minimal counterexample `${}` -- the reference emits a span, the prototype emitted none. The memo is unsound twice: a position reached with a different owed is not interchangeable, and marking every visited position failed is wrong because the walk also includes positions that were merely skipped.

attempts.idea: Per-family event tables built in the reference's exact stepping order, closure by scanning the closer list.
attempts.outcome: REJECTED. Closest of the five; the residual errors were in the closer-consumption rule, e.g. `{{{}}}` where the reference closes at 6 and this closed at 5.

attempts.idea: Same event tables with a baseline taken as the cumulative owed before the first event at or after the scan start.
attempts.outcome: REJECTED. Off-by-one in the baseline: the cumulative owed BEFORE an event is not the owed AFTER the previous one, because the scan start is not event-aligned.

attempts.idea: Binary search over the cumulative owed sequence at closer events.
attempts.outcome: REJECTED. Binary searching a quantity that is not the search key. Two index corrections were tried (cum[mid] versus cum[mid+1]) and neither reached equivalence, which is the signal that the formulation is wrong rather than the arithmetic.

attempts.idea: Precomputed close-map (brace stack + dollar-paren stack) with lookup by opener position.
attempts.outcome: REJECTED. Minimal counterexample `${}`. The balance observation is sound; the lookup indexing was wrong, and it was wrong on the simplest case in the family.

algorithm_search.structural_finding: The reason these formulations fail is now quantified: the peak of `owed` during a scan grows LINEARLY with the input -- 1026 at n=1024 and 4098 at n=4096 for `'{'.repeat(n)`, 2050 at n=4096 for `'${{ '.repeat(n/4)`. So a state table indexed by (position, owed) is O(n^2) in memory and is not available, and any approach that hopes a single derived key (a threshold, a monotone scan position) captures the state is collapsing a two-dimensional state space into one dimension. That is also why the monotonicity conjecture in attempt 3-of-the-earlier-round was falsified: several owed values coexist at one position.
algorithm_search.what_remains: The two-dimensional state is irreducible as stated, so the fix has to change WHAT is computed rather than how it is looked up: either (a) an explicit stack machine that emits constructs as they close while keeping failed outer attempts from consuming inner candidates -- which is the design the task asked for and is a real piece of work, or (b) a documented parser resource limit, which is a mitigation and must NOT be reported as this finding fixed.
algorithm_search.interim_mitigation: R3-REDOS-003 (trailing-trim) was found in the same sweep and IS fixed; it was an independent cubic term. The unclosed-opener family remains the dominant remaining cost at 32 KiB.
algorithm_search.recommendation: Do not attempt a sixth formulation under time pressure. Attempt 3 reached 9 differences out of 111111 and is the best starting point for a stack machine: its event-table construction in the reference's stepping order is correct, and only the closure search needs to be replaced by a stack that tracks the live owed values.

close_map_attempt.idea: Precompute, once per document, the closing position of every relevant opener -- a brace balance stack for ${{ / {{ / ${ and a $(-only stack for $( -- then answer each complex opener with an O(1)/O(log n) lookup. Structurally different from attempts 1-5: it does not compress owed state, does not assume monotonicity, does not memoise failure, and does not change the scanner stepping semantics.
close_map_attempt.outcome: REJECTED by the repo oracle. Minimal counterexample `${}` -- the reference emits start=0 end=3 and the prototype emitted nothing.
close_map_attempt.what_was_established: The underlying observation is CORRECT and worth keeping: for a brace-family opener the owed net change is equivalent to an ordinary brace balance, and the close point satisfies 'the first `}` at which the running balance drops by `delimiter` OR MORE relative to the opener's end'. That formula reproduced every value I traced by hand -- 5 for `${{}}`, 4 for `{{}}`, 3 for `${}`, 6 for `{{{}}}`, -1 for `${{}`, 14 for `${{ a: {b:1}}}`. The prototype failed on a smaller, non-mathematical detail: the lookup was anchored on the balance sequence indexed by closing-bracket positions, and choosing the comparison at that index is off by one in a way that a formula sanity-check does not catch. It failed `${}` -- the simplest possible brace-family case -- which is how the whole attempt should have been tested first.
close_map_attempt.lesson: I verified the formula against hand-traced values and then wrote the lookup against a differently-indexed sequence, and treated the first as evidence for the second. Two hand-checked examples would have caught it immediately; the exhaustive oracle did, which is why the oracle is the gate and not the arithmetic.

algorithm_search.decision: STOPPED per the agreed rule: no seventh formulation. Seven attempts (five lookup formulations plus predecessor-chain memoisation plus the close-map) have now each been measured against the 111111-string oracle and none reached equivalence. R3-REDOS-002 remains an OPEN, release-blocking availability finding, and work moves to R3.4 (depth/stack) and R3.6 (soak), which are not blocked by it. A dedicated parser-design block is the right place for the stack machine, and attempt 3's event tables remain the best foundation for it.

findings.term_quantification: Two separate quadratic terms were measured so the fix targets the right one. (a) The balanced scan dominates: unclosed openers cost 73/270/1196ms at 4096/8192/16384 with |out| = 0. (b) The final containment filter `out.filter((env) => !out.some(...))` is O(|out|^2) but is SECOND ORDER here: 3276 sibling envelopes cost 41.8ms total, so the filter accounts for roughly 0.3%. Optimising the filter would not address the reported finding.
findings.recommendation: Do not start an eighth formulation in this session. R3-REDOS-002 must appear in the release notes as an open release-blocking availability finding with a reproducible reproducer, the measured scaling, and the seven rejected approaches, so the next attempt starts from evidence rather than from a blank page. The stack machine remains the intended design, built on attempt 3's event tables, and accepted only against the 111111-string oracle plus a seeded differential over >=100k longer strings.

findings.input: 'k' + ' '.repeat(n - 2) + ':'   -- one character, a long run of spaces, a colon
findings.config: any flag set; parseYamlBindings() runs on every document
findings.expected_invariant: Trimming trailing whitespace from a line is a linear walk from the end. No single-line operation may cost superlinear time.
findings.observed: `line.replace(/\s+$/, "")` -- and `replace(/[ \t]+$/, "")` just as badly -- is QUADRATIC on a long trailing run: the greedy `+` tries the longest run, fails the end anchor, then retries one character shorter, so O(n) attempts per line. In a document split into many lines whose total length is n, one long line makes it O(n^2) and many lines make it O(n^3). Measured through parseYamlBindings on 'k' + spaces + ':': 7.32ms at 2 KB, 113ms at 8 KB, 1806ms at 32 KB, with the doubling ratio holding at ~16.
findings.impact: Availability / DoS, and the most reachable of the three regex findings: no special characters are needed, only a long run of spaces followed by a colon. It runs on every request regardless of which detectors are enabled, and it showed up as amplifying adversarial/control ratios in the sweep (10.36 -> 22.80 -> 48.68).
findings.root_cause: Greedy quantifier plus end anchor in a trailing-trim regex. The engine cannot know the run length without trying, and each failed attempt is re-anchored at the end of the string.
findings.fix: stripTrailing(text, isStrip) walks backwards once and stops at the first character outside the set. Both regex forms are replaced, not only the `\s` one, because `[ \t]+$` measured just as badly (1985ms at 32768). `String.prototype.trimEnd()` would also be linear but strips a fixed Unicode set, so a character walk was used instead to keep each call site's exact set. Four sites: parseYamlBindings' trimmedEnd, the block-scalar region end, the block-scalar body line, and splitPlainScalar's value. Equivalence was checked EXHAUSTIVELY against both original regexes over every string of length 0..4 on a 9-character alphabet including NBSP and ideographic space: 7381/7381 identical. Measured after the fix at 32 KB: 1806ms -> 3.43ms.
findings.regression: scripts/perf-redos.mjs family A-assignment-delimiter, whose adversarial/control ratio is the detector for this class.
findings.measurement_note: This finding was NOT in a regex I suspected. The YAML mapping pattern, `([^\s:#][^:#]*?)[ \t]*:`, does contain an ambiguous nested quantifier and measured 0.044ms -- innocent. Isolating each STEP of the same line (exec, trimEnd, dash-strip) is what located the real cost.

findings.input: a request body larger than REDACT_MAX_BODY_BYTES, in four Content-Length shapes: declared oversized, absent, understated, and overstated-but-small
findings.expected_invariant: Split into two layers. SEMANTIC: an oversized body never reaches JSON.parse, redaction or the upstream forward -- that already held. RESOURCE: the read stops once the cap is exceeded instead of materialising the body first.
findings.observed: `await request.arrayBuffer()` read the WHOLE body before any size check could run, so all 200055 bytes were materialised and only then answered 413 -- including when Content-Length had already declared the body oversized. The 415 content-type check had the same shape. Measured with a 1024-byte chunk source: deliveredBytes == totalBytes in every refused case.
findings.impact: Resource / deployment robustness. No security consequence: the semantic limit held, so no oversized body was parsed, redacted or forwarded, and an untrue Content-Length could not move the cap in either direction. The exposure is memory only, and the request was refused either way.
findings.root_cause: The size check ran after the buffering call rather than during the read.
findings.fix: readBodyCapped() pulls from request.body chunk by chunk, counts, and on exceeding the cap calls reader.cancel() and returns. cancel() is what makes the saving real: without it the rest of the stream may still be transported and buffered by the runtime. Content-Length is deliberately NOT used as the boundary -- it can be absent or untrue -- so it remains at most an early hint and the counted read is the enforcement. Measured after: deliveredBytes 1024 of 200055 in all three refused shapes, cancelled=true, status 413, upstream 0.
findings.regression: test/r35-limits.test.js -- L1 across four Content-Length shapes and a huge non-JSON body; L4 requiring deliveredBytes <= 2 chunks AND < total AND cancelled; L5 that an understated header cannot smuggle an oversized body through and an overstated one cannot refuse a body that fits; L2 boundary precision at exactly the cap and one byte over; L3 that a huge non-JSON body fails the SIZE check rather than the content-type check.
findings.found_via: Reading the production path (arrayBuffer -> check) and then measuring, rather than assuming. The measurement required counting bytes DELIVERED TO THE READER: an earlier probe counted what the source had queued, which reports the whole body regardless and would have hidden the finding.

findings.input: 10000 candidates with 1 unique plaintext, versus 100 unique, versus 10000 unique; and 1000 candidates / 1 unique against 1000 / 1000
findings.config: REDACT_MAX_REDACTIONS=1 versus 1000000 on the same document
findings.expected_invariant: A limit named MAX_REDACTIONS and documented as something to lower on memory-constrained deployments should bound the work of processing candidates, not only the allocation that follows it.
findings.observed: Two results. (1) SEMANTICS: the limit is `rawToToken.size`, so it bounds UNIQUE ENTITY IDENTITIES -- not spans and not occurrences. Measured: 200 spans over 2 unique values passes a limit of 2 (rawToToken.size 2), while 5 spans over 5 unique values trips a limit of 2. The boundary is exact: limit=N admits exactly N unique values. (2) TIMING: the differential between maxRedactions=1 and maxRedactions=1000000 is 0.63-0.95, i.e. the expensive stages cost the same either way. A 10000-candidate document still spends 3.8s before the limit fires and 5.1s when it does not. findSensitiveSpans runs its parsers, detectors, envelopes and merge BEFORE the first tokenFor, so the limit cannot influence any of it.
findings.impact: Documentation and contract mismatch, with no security consequence. L1 holds: a request that trips the limit is answered 413 with upstreamFetch 0, and the failure throws so no partial document is returned. The problem is that SECURITY.md and README.md present lowering REDACT_MAX_REDACTIONS as a memory-constrained-deployment knob, which reads as a resource guard. It is an entity-allocation and output limit; CPU and memory before the first mint are unaffected by it. Severity Low / docs.
findings.recommendation: Keep the mechanism, fix the description: state that it caps distinct entity identities and that it takes effect at the minting stage, so it does not bound candidate processing. The name MAX_REDACTIONS was accurate for its semantics but invites the wrong reading; a comment and doc line should say which stage it fires at. Any actual CPU bound would be a separate candidate-count or time budget enforced BEFORE the merge.
findings.regression: test/r35-limits.test.js -- the unique-versus-span-versus-occurrence distinction, the exact boundary for limits 1/2/3/5, fail-closed with no partial output, 413 with no upstream fetch, and an explicit L4 test recording that maxRedactions does NOT bound the pre-mint stages (asserting the span set is a function of the document, not of the limit).
findings.verification: The sweep this replaces was a same-document differential, which is what makes the timing claim a measurement rather than an inference from source order.
findings.fix: Documentation only; production behaviour unchanged and the configuration name kept. README.md now describes REDACT_MAX_BODY_BYTES as a hard cap on request-body bytes consumed, with an oversized read cancelled before JSON parsing or redaction, and REDACT_MAX_REDACTIONS as the maximum number of unique plaintext identities minted in one request, bounding request-local mapping and output allocation but NOT detector candidate count or pre-mint CPU work. The 'lower REDACT_MAX_BODY_BYTES and/or REDACT_MAX_REDACTIONS' sentence now separates the two: the body cap is the deployment knob, and the entity cap is explicitly not a detector/merge CPU budget, with the stage it is consulted at spelled out. SECURITY.md checklist item 3 was rewritten the same way, including that it is not a substitute for the body cap and cannot shorten the work a document full of candidates causes.
findings.classification: fixed: documentation / contract clarification; production behavior unchanged

findings.input: a non-stream upstream response larger than any configured bound
findings.expected_invariant: If a request body has a size limit, the analogous response path should be documented as having one too, or the absence should be stated.
findings.observed: The non-stream response path calls `await upstreamResponse.text()`, which materialises the entire textual response, and there is no REDACT_MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES or equivalent. A request body is bounded; the response is not. The SSE path is separate and streams.
findings.impact: Deployment robustness gap, recorded as an OBSERVATION rather than a finding: no documentation promises a response limit, so nothing is contradicted. The asymmetry is still worth knowing, because a deployment sizing memory from REDACT_MAX_BODY_BYTES would be sizing only half the path.
findings.recommendation: Either add a response size bound with the same capped-read treatment as the request side, or state in the deployment notes that response buffering is unbounded and the upstream is expected to be trusted for response size. Do not treat this as an implementation bug until a limit is actually promised.
findings.verdict: NO RESPONSE CAP ADDED. The condition set for adding one was a clear memory amplification, a high peak, a latency cliff, or large responses easily causing resource pressure. None appeared.

r3_3_measurements.binary_passthrough: 16M 51.0ms, 314 MiB/s, peakRSS 152MiB, no parse or policy work at all
r3_3_measurements.sse: 16M 461.4ms, 34.7 MiB/s, peakRSS 306MiB, ratios 1.46-2.69; slower per byte than non-stream JSON because every event is parsed and walked individually, which is the price of not buffering

findings.reasoning: The triggering condition was explicit: add a cap only if a 16 MiB textual response showed obvious amplification, an excessive peak, a latency cliff, or easy resource pressure. Measured amplification is 13.6x peak RSS on the worst path, scaling stays linear with x4 ratios under 2, and throughput RISES with size (4.3 -> 104 MiB/s for JSON), which is the opposite of a cliff. A response cap would therefore be a new public runtime policy -- with its own status code, default value and binary/SSE semantics -- added without a measured problem to justify it. The asymmetry with the request side is now documented rather than enforced.

findings.input: JSON.stringify({ model:'g', messages:[{role:'user',content:'hi'}], deep: <object chain of depth 2300> })  -- roughly 14 KB
findings.config: default deployment configuration; flags irrelevant (the overflow happens in the structural walk, before any detector)
findings.expected_invariant: The agreed R3.4 contract: depth <= 128 completes normally; beyond that a request may succeed OR be rejected in a CONTROLLED way; never a raw RangeError, uncaught exception, 500, or partial mutation.
findings.observed: handleRequest THROWS an uncaught RangeError ('Maximum call stack size exceeded') for a ~14 KB body, upstream fetch count 0. The recursion is redactJson's structural walk. Boundary measured on a FRESH node process, first call, three repetitions per point: 2200 ok, 2300 RangeError, for object chains, array chains and alternating chains alike. JSON.parse itself handles 2500 fine, so the limit is the gateway's own recursion rather than the JSON parser.
findings.impact: Availability / attacker-controlled 500. The trigger is ~14 KB of ordinary JSON, trivially inside the 16 MiB body cap and requiring no special characters. It fails CLOSED -- no upstream fetch, so no plaintext leaves the gateway -- and no confidentiality fail-open was found. Severity Medium by the R3.4 classification: a shallow attacker-controlled JSON reliably produces a production 500 rather than a clean refusal.
findings.contract_status: The depth contract itself is SATISFIED and by a wide margin: 128 is required and 2200 works, 17x the requirement. What is violated is the SEPARATE invariant that a limit must be expressed as a controlled rejection rather than a raw exception. These are two different claims and should not be conflated -- the second is fixable without touching the first.
findings.measurement_note: The boundary is only reproducible on the FIRST call in a fresh process. Ten sequential calls in one process gave four RangeErrors followed by six successes, because V8's stack check and tiering change after the function has overflowed once. Any depth figure quoted from a warmed-up process is meaningless; every data point here came from a separate `node` invocation.
findings.recommendation: Add ONE structural depth guard shared by all four recursive paths -- redactJson, restoreJson, applyOperandPolicy, restoreCompleteStrings -- rather than four independently invented limits. Placed at the entry point it also saves doing the parse-and-walk work before refusing. A limit around 512 would be 4x the required 128 and far below the measured 2200, so it cannot refuse anything the contract requires. NOT implemented yet: the boundary is high, the failure is fail-closed, and where a guard belongs is a design decision rather than a defect repair.
findings.regression: test/r34-depth.test.js -- depth 1/32/64/128 on both paths for three container shapes; guard exactness at 511/512/513; 413 with no upstream fetch for an over-deep request; 502 for an over-deep response; an over-deep SSE event becoming a stream error with the reader cancelled; the guard surviving a 100000-deep chain without throwing; and THE ONE THAT MATTERS, an over-deep untrusted tool operand containing an OWN token must never expose its plaintext, at depths 513/1000/2800/3200, with a counterpart test proving a shallow operand is still preserved and a trusted one still resolved.
findings.severity: RE-CLASSIFIED High / release-blocking SECURITY (sink-policy fail-open). Originally Medium availability only; the fail-open probe changed that.

fail_open.how_found: The requested follow-up probe. restoreNonStreamResponse wrapped JSON.parse, applyResponsePolicy AND JSON.stringify in ONE try, and the catch re-processed the WHOLE raw response under the assistant_text policy -- which RESOLVES tokens.
fail_open.exploit: An upstream non-stream Anthropic response whose content[] carries a tool_use with an untrusted tool name and an input nested deeper than the walker's stack allows. The RangeError from applyOperandPolicy is caught, the raw response text is treated as assistant prose, and the OWN token sitting inside the untrusted tool operand is substituted with its plaintext.
fail_open.measured_before: Fresh process, 3/3 per depth: depth 2500 -> status 200, token preserved, no plaintext; depth 2800 -> status 200, PLAINTEXT LEAKED, token gone; depth 3000 and 3200 the same.
fail_open.measured_after: depth 513, 2800 and 3200 -> status 502, no plaintext, 3/3 each. The over-deep response is refused before the policy walk.
fail_open.why_this_is_high: A confidentiality fail-open reached through an attacker-influenced upstream response, with the plaintext placed specifically in a channel the sink policy exists to protect. It also inverted the intended behaviour: the deeper the nesting, the LESS protection.

findings.fix: Two parts, both required. (1) NARROW THE CATCH: only JSON.parse failures may take the inert-text fallback; applyResponsePolicy is no longer inside the try, so a policy or traversal failure propagates and fails closed instead of silently downgrading to assistant_text. (2) ONE STRUCTURAL DEPTH GUARD, exceedsJsonDepth(value, 512), non-recursive by construction (a guard that recursed would overflow on the input it exists to catch). Applied at the three real production boundaries: the request path after JSON.parse and before redactJson (413, no upstream fetch), the non-stream response after JSON.parse and before applyResponsePolicy (502, since the upstream call already happened), and the SSE path before streamFields (which itself recurses), where an over-deep event becomes a stream error, the offending event is not emitted, and the upstream reader is cancelled. applyOperandPolicy needs no second check because its caller has already validated.
findings.measured_after: Request path fresh process: depth 2200/2300/2800 all ok -- the V8 boundary is no longer production-reachable because the guard fires at 513. Guard boundary exact: body depth 511 and 512 pass, 513 is refused, identically for object, array and alternating chains.
findings.implementation_note: A first attempt at the SSE guard accumulated whole events and re-emitted them, which destroyed the streaming contract -- 20 SSE tests failed because chunks no longer corresponded to upstream chunks. It is now a pure PASS-THROUGH: every chunk is forwarded unchanged and the guard only observes. A second mistake was dropping restoreSseStream from the SSE return path while wiring the guard, which silently disabled token restoration entirely; the failing suite caught both.

findings.input: JSON.stringify({model:'g',messages:[{role:'user',content:'x'.repeat(n)}]})  with n from 64 KiB to 16 MiB
findings.config: default configuration (gitleaks + highEntropy on); no secrets anywhere in the body
findings.expected_invariant: Cost must scale with the body size, not with its square. The shipped body cap is 16 MiB, so a request AT the cap must be processable in a time a request handler can afford.
findings.observed: Measured on a request body containing no secrets and no special structure: 64 KiB 30.6ms, 256 KiB 60.9ms (ratio 1.99), 1 MiB 234ms (3.84), 4 MiB 946ms (4.04), 16 MiB 3879ms (4.10). The curve is linear up to ~256 KiB and quadratic from ~1 MiB, so a legal maximum-size body costs 3.9 seconds of CPU. Because a body is walked once per request, that is the per-request cost of accepting a large legitimate payload, not an adversarial-only path -- the adversarial version is simply that it is trivial to send.
findings.impact: Availability / CPU. A single 16 MiB request occupies a worker for ~4 seconds; a handful of concurrent ones exhaust a small deployment. No confidentiality impact. Severity Medium-High for a gateway whose own configuration advertises 16 MiB as supported.
findings.blocking: R3.3 body-size scaling cannot produce a meaningful baseline until this is understood, because the corpus sizes it needs are exactly the range where the cost becomes quadratic. Recorded first, measured second, fixed third -- per the R3 rule of not starting a rewrite from a symptom.
findings.localisation_so_far: Narrowed but NOT concluded. (a) The four structured-context parsers are LINEAR: parseBindings 1M 4.2ms / 2M 8.1 / 4M 16.2, parseYamlBindings 2.4/4.5/9.1. (b) referenceEnvelopes on 4 MiB of 'x' is 262ms and linear -- it is the known open R3-REDOS-002 family, which the task correctly said not to mix into the body baseline; it is nonetheless a contributor at these sizes and must be subtracted when localising. (c) Instrumenting collectGitleakSpans per rule shows the most expensive single rule is 4.4ms at 256 KiB and that the bulk is spread across ~1200 rules, each doing a `lower.includes(keyword)` pre-filter against the WHOLE text -- 1200 full scans of a 4 MiB string is 4.8 G character comparisons, which is the shape of the cost. That is a plausible primary term, NOT yet proven to be the only one.
findings.next_step: Measure, fresh process per point, on the same 4 MiB and 16 MiB clean corpus: G off, structured parsers off, H off, reference envelopes isolated, and the full pipeline. Then compute phase_time/total_time. Only a phase with a significant share is worth touching.
findings.measurement_note: Scaling is the primary signal and absolute ms is recorded. Every point came from a single process invocation; the curve was reproduced for 'x'*n, lorem text, short config lines and URL-heavy text, so it is not an artefact of one corpus.
findings.severity: Observation -- throughput / constant factor, NOT a complexity finding
findings.correction: WITHDRAWN AS A COMPLEXITY FINDING. My ratios were computed correctly but INTERPRETED against the wrong doubling base: the size sequence is 64K -> 256K -> 1M -> 4M -> 16M, i.e. x4 per step, so a LINEAR algorithm is expected to show T(4n)/T(n) ~ 4. The measured tail 3.84 / 4.04 / 4.10 gives p = log(ratio)/log(4) ~ 0.97 / 1.01 / 1.02, which is linear. Genuine O(n^2) on this sequence would approach 16. This is the sixth time in this session that an unverified inference of mine was written down as a conclusion; the specific failure here is applying x2 reasoning to a x4 series.
findings.restated: The real question is throughput, not complexity: a legal 16 MiB body costs about 3.9s of CPU, i.e. ~4.1 MiB/s for a clean request. Whether that is acceptable is a product question about constant factors, and the implementation is linear either way.
findings.phase_attribution_required_before_any_op: Measure, fresh process per point, on the same 4 MiB and 16 MiB clean corpus: G off, structured parsers off, H off, reference envelopes isolated, and the full pipeline. Then compute phase_time/total_time. Only a phase with a significant share is worth touching.
findings.note_on_gitleaks: The keyword pre-filter `for (rule of rules) rule.keywords.some(k => lower.includes(k))` is O(ruleCount x n), which is LINEAR in n for a fixed rule set, with a possibly large constant. It must NOT be described as this round's quadratic term. It is only worth rewriting if instrumentation shows it dominates -- and a multi-pattern scan such as Aho-Corasick would then need a differential against the current function comparing start/end/ruleId/ORDER over overlapping keywords, prefix keywords, punctuation keywords, case folding, keyword-less rules and repeated keywords. Not before it is proven dominant, and not as a giant regex.

phase_attribution.method: Fresh process per point. Each candidate disabled in turn on the SAME clean corpus, then phase_time/total_time.
phase_attribution.conclusion: ms/MiB is essentially flat (239 -> 244) and every phase keeps the same share across a 4x size increase, so the scaling is healthy and the issue is a constant factor. Detectors are 99.3% of the work; JSON.parse is 0.4%. The single largest contributor is the gitleaks family at ~80%, within which the keyword pre-filter is the dominant term: ~1200 rules each running `lower.includes(keyword)` over the whole body. At 16 MiB that is ~6 GB/s of memory traffic, which is bandwidth-bound rather than algorithmically expensive -- hence linear with a large constant. referenceEnvelopes is a consistent 27-28% and is the known open R3-REDOS-002 family.
phase_attribution.next_step: Optimising is now justified by measurement rather than by inspection, and the target is the gitleaks keyword pre-filter: one multi-pattern pass computing the set of keywords PRESENT, instead of one full-text scan per rule. Any such rewrite must be differential against the current collectGitleakSpans comparing start/end/ruleId AND ORDER, over overlapping keywords, prefix keywords, punctuation keywords, case folding, keyword-less rules and repeated keywords. NOT started in this round, and explicitly not as a giant regex.

findings.input: parser-heavy config text: N lines of `service_i: { host: svc-i.internal, port: 1000+i, password: "${VAULT_i}" }` joined by newlines, wrapped in a request body
findings.config: default detectors; measured per detector in a FRESH process with the others disabled and structuredContext off
findings.expected_invariant: Cost must scale with input size. On a x4 size sequence a linear pass shows T(4n)/T(n) ~ 4.
findings.observed: SUPERLINEAR, and unlike R3-BODY-001 this is not a misread base -- the sequence is x4 and the ratios are 7.7 and 9.9, well above 4: gitleaks 222.3ms / 1377.8ms / 10632.3ms at 256K / 1M / 4M (1377.8 -> 10632.3 is 7.7x), highEntropy 201.0 / 1119.5 / 11039.1 (9.9x). Both detectors exceed 10 SECONDS at 4 MiB on this corpus. The same detectors measured on a 4 MiB body of plain 'x' cost 758ms and 477ms respectively, so the cost is a function of the INPUT SHAPE, not of detector setup or of size alone.
findings.impact: Availability / CPU, and worse than R3-BODY-001: a few hundred KiB of structured config text already costs seconds, and the linear-extrapolated 16 MiB cost is minutes. Config-shaped text is exactly what this gateway is expected to relay, so this is a realistic payload rather than a contrived one. No confidentiality impact.
findings.blocking: R3.3 corpus B (parser-heavy) cannot be measured to 16 MiB until this is understood; the 8 MiB point already took 37 seconds and 16 MiB did not complete inside 60 seconds. Corpus A (clean) and the response-side corpora are unaffected and their baselines are valid.

localisation_so_far.ruled_out: The four structured-context parsers are LINEAR on this exact corpus: at 4 MiB parseBindings 39.0ms, parseYamlBindings 103.6ms, parseHeaderBindings 18.4ms, parseUrlBindings 1.7ms -- 163ms total, which cannot explain 10 seconds.
localisation_so_far.ruled_out_2: JSON.parse is 0.4% of the work on the clean corpus and the same order here.
localisation_so_far.suspected: Something inside the detector loops that is sensitive to the NUMBER of alphanumeric blocks or of candidate matches rather than to byte count. The corpus produces ZERO spans (G=0, entropy=0, binding=0), so the merge and the token path are not involved at all -- this is entirely inside the two detector functions. For highEntropy the natural candidate is the per-block scoring path (tokenizeBlocks plus shannonEntropy/entropyScore per block) and for gitleaks the candidate post-filtering path, but NEITHER has been measured yet and this record explicitly does not claim either.
localisation_so_far.measurement_caveat: Enabling ALL detectors measured FASTER than gitleaks alone on the same corpus (9351ms vs 11184ms at 4 MiB). That is not possible for additive work and means the isolated single-flag numbers are themselves affected by something other than pure work -- most likely GC pressure and allocation behaviour differing with the total allocation volume. Every number here therefore needs re-measurement before it is used for a decision, and the ordering must not be read as a ranking.

findings.next_step: Instrument inside the two detector functions on this corpus: count tokenizeBlocks output, time the per-block scoring loop, count candidate matches per rule, and time the post-match filtering. Fresh process per point. Then localise before any change -- the same rule that produced two wrong guesses this session already.
findings.measurement_note: Every point came from a separate process invocation with only one flag enabled. The corpus generator is deterministic and is recorded in full so the reproducer is exact.
findings.severity: Medium (availability / CPU amplification), root cause isolated

attribution.question: Is the superlinearity (A) the WORK COUNT growing superlinearly or (B) the work count staying linear while the PER-UNIT cost grows with n?
attribution.answer: (B), and the per-unit cost is now located exactly.
attribution.probe_1_isolated_referenceEnvelopes: 256K envs=3278 (13110/MiB) 189.1ms ; 1M envs=12835 (12834/MiB) 1168.2ms ; 4M envs=49843 (12461/MiB) 9706.7ms. envs/MiB is FLAT -- the work count is linear -- while ms/MiB rises 756 -> 1168 -> 2427.
attribution.probe_2_same_length_control: The identical corpus with `${VAULT_i}` replaced by the equal-length `X{VAULT i}` (whose body cannot match the simple `{name}` construct because it contains a space): envs=0 at every size, and 24.9ms / 80.5ms / 284.2ms with ms/MiB FALLING 99 -> 81 -> 71. Linear, so the cost is the reference constructs and not the corpus shape.
attribution.probe_3_split_and_bypass: Instrumented the two halves of referenceEnvelopes separately and then bypassed the filter. At 4 MiB: scanner 271.8ms, containment filter 9532.4ms, total 9804.6ms; with the filter bypassed the whole function is 276.9ms. The filter is 97% of it, and raw == kept (49843 == 49843, i.e. NOTHING is actually contained in this corpus), so the quadratic work is pure waste here.
attribution.prediction_check: The hypothesis predicted 9.7s before measurement, from 41.8ms at 3276 envelopes scaled as (50000/3276)^2. Measured filter time at 49843 envelopes: 9.53s. The agreement is close enough that the mechanism is not in doubt.

findings.root_cause: PROVEN: referenceEnvelopes() final containment filter, O(|out|^2) in the number of reference envelopes.
findings.withdrawn: WITHDRAWN: my previous statement that the cost sits 'between H tokenization and scoring'. That measurement was made through the FULL findSensitiveSpans(), and referenceEnvelopes() is called unconditionally at worker.js:2867 -- it is NOT gated by structuredContext, so setting structuredContext:false does not remove it. The H-only run therefore still contained the reference work and was never detector-local. The block counters were still valid as counters; the attribution drawn from that run was not.
findings.relationship_to_redos_002: Same function, DIFFERENT failure mode, and the two must not be merged unless one fix happens to cover both. R3-REDOS-002: unclosed constructs, |out| = 0, dominant cost is the repeated FAILED forward scan. R3-BODY-002: many legal sibling constructs, |out| large, dominant cost is the final containment filter O(|out|^2), with the scanner itself linear.
findings.fix_scope: Narrower than REDOS-002 and does NOT require touching the reference parsing or its fallback semantics: only the step 'drop envelopes fully contained in another' needs an equivalent reduction. Acceptance must be an EXACT-ARRAY differential (start/end/opener/order) against the current implementation, since the filter is the only thing being replaced.
findings.secondary_watch_item: worker.js:2868 keys a `documentReferences` array and then scans it per span, i.e. O(spans x |constructs|). Its own comment already records this as second order and calls a bounds-keyed memo the next step 'if a document with many constructs and many spans ever shows up in a profile'. Corpus B is exactly that document -- 49843 constructs and a span per line -- so this term must be measured as part of the fix, not after it.

phase_1_result.hypothesis: The scanner jumps to envelope.end on every success and advances by one on every failure, so `out` should be sorted and strictly DISJOINT -- in which case the final containment filter can never remove anything and is a no-op that should be DELETED rather than rewritten.
phase_1_result.verdict: PROVEN. The filter is an identity and has been removed.

evidence.exhaustive: Every string of length 0..5 on the 10-character alphabet { } $ ( ) % < > x _ = 111111 strings: raw != filtered in 0 cases, overlapping in 0, contained in 0.
evidence.seeded: 120000 pseudo-random strings of length 1..64 on a 20-character alphabet including whitespace and newlines: 0 differences, 0 overlaps, 0 containments.
evidence.targeted: 18 shapes -- sibling constructs, adjacent `${a}${b}`, nested `${{ a: {b:1}}}`, failed-outer-then-inner `{{x}` and `${({}`, mixed families, unmatched closers, unclosed-then-valid, simple-adjacent-complex, the three falsified-monotonicity shapes, token-like text, a multi-line construct, 200 siblings, and a construct-free document: 0 differences.
evidence.corpus_B_at_scale: 3278 / 12835 / 49843 envelopes -- raw == filtered at every size, overlap false, contained false.
evidence.nested_counter_check: The closest thing to a counterexample, `${{ a: {b:1}}}`, yields a SINGLE envelope [0,14,'${{'] -- the scanner's own balanced scan already consumed the inner construct, so there is nothing left to contain.

phase_1_result.why_disjointness_follows: On success the scanner sets i = envelope.end, so the next envelope starts at or after the previous one's end; on failure it advances i by 1 while pushing nothing. Every pushed envelope therefore begins at or after the previous pushed envelope's end, which makes `out` sorted and non-overlapping by construction. Containment requires overlap, so containment is impossible.
phase_1_result.measurement_method_note: The overlap check was widened from adjacent-pairs to FULL PAIRS before the verdict: adjacent disjointness alone would not establish identity, because the filter removes on containment and only full pairwise disjointness rules that out. One prototype defect was found and fixed while doing this: the early-return for empty input skipped the instrumentation entirely and left the probe reading undefined, which would have looked like a crash rather than a silent gap.

findings.fix: DELETE the final containment filter. Chosen over rewriting it as an O(n log n) sweep or interval tree, because a step that provably never changes its input should be removed rather than made faster. This is also strictly safer than a rewrite: any behaviour the filter was accidentally providing would surface immediately as an exact-array differential failure, whereas an equivalent-but-different algorithm could mask a semantic difference.

Making it free means moving the call behind the emptiness test, which is a separate change and was not made.

findings.regression: test/b2-containment.test.js pins the INVARIANT rather than the deletion: envelopes sorted and strictly disjoint across 18 shapes and a 2000-construct corpus; no envelope contained in another over the 111111-string exhaustive corpus; the nested `${{ a: {b:1}}}` case yielding a single envelope; and a bounded linearity check on 4x the construct count. The linearity check is there because correctness alone CANNOT catch this class of defect -- the deleted filter never changed the result, so every other assertion passed while the function was 36x slower than necessary.

findings.input: documents where no detector produces a surviving span, including one reference construct per line
findings.expected_invariant: Stages that only ADJUST existing spans must not run when there are no spans. reference widening, infra widening, the remerge and applyObjectSchema all fit that description.
findings.observed: referenceEnvelopes(text) was called unconditionally BEFORE anything tested whether there was anything to widen, so on an input with no detector hit it was the most expensive part of the call. It is not free to skip by accident: the call site sits above the `padded.length === 0` condition, not below it.
findings.impact: Constant-factor only, no security consequence. Measured on corpus B (zero spans): 4 MiB findSensitiveSpans 1240.9ms -> 946.5ms, i.e. it removes the ~267ms the reference scan was costing on an input that never used its result. ms/MiB stayed flat (368 -> 296 -> 237 -> 229 -> 236).
findings.fix: Return early when `padded.length === 0`, placed AFTER the coverage-bearing parsers have run and BEFORE referenceEnvelopes. The coverage contract is preserved rather than short-circuited: `const empty = []; return coverage ? coverage.attachTo(empty) : empty;` -- returning a bare [] would silently drop coverage on exactly the inputs where coverage matters most, a document the detectors found nothing in.
findings.differential: Exact comparison against the pre-change implementation, over 14 case/flag combinations covering all four requested shapes: no detector hit with many valid refs, no detector hit with malformed/unclosed refs, no detector hit on ordinary clean text, and WITH a hit so the fast path must not fire. Compared spans by start/end/type/priority/ruleId/classifiedText/evidence, the coverage summary, and the ARRAY'S OWN PROPERTY NAMES (the returned array carries a non-enumerable coverage property). 0 differences. Run twice, once against HEAD and once against the pre-BODY-002 commit 1aad949, so the check also proves that Phase 1 and Phase 3 together are equivalent to the behaviour before either change.
findings.explicitly_not_a_fix_for_redos_002: This narrows R3-REDOS-002's reachability but must NOT be recorded as fixing it. The moment a single span survives, referenceEnvelopes() runs again and the repeated failed forward scan over unclosed constructs is unchanged. A document with one secret and one unclosed construct still pays it.
findings.regression: Covered by the existing coverage and reference suites; the differential above is the acceptance evidence.
findings.config: default detectors; corpus B (one reference construct per line, zero surviving spans)
findings.note_on_id: The Phase 3 fast path, recorded as its own finding because it is a separate change from the Phase 1 filter deletion and neither implies the other.

findings.input: m lines of `cfg_i: { svc: "svc-i", token: "${VAULT_i}", cred: "<secret>" }` -- one reference construct AND one surviving span per line, so envelopeFor() is genuinely called m times and each call scans m references
findings.config: gitleaks + highEntropy on; m from 500 to 16000
findings.expected_invariant: The span-to-envelope lookup must not cost O(spans x references). Measured as T(2m)/T(m): linear would be ~2.
findings.observed: SUPERLINEAR and worsening: 500 38.2ms, 1000 77.2ms (2.02x), 2000 229.3ms (2.97x), 4000 719.9ms (3.14x), 8000 1815.5ms (2.52x), 16000 8785.8ms (4.84x). Per-unit cost rises 76 -> 77 -> 115 -> 180 -> 227 -> 549 us per line. At 16000 constructs with 16000 surviving spans the call takes 8.8 SECONDS.
findings.impact: Availability / CPU. A config-shaped document with a few thousand lines is ordinary for this gateway, and thousands of distinct secrets in one request reaches the same place. Note this is a DIFFERENT defect from R3-BODY-002: that one was the containment filter over the envelope list alone (fixed, and it fired even with ZERO spans); this one needs BOTH many references AND many surviving spans, and it lives in the per-span lookup at worker.js:2868.
findings.separate_from_body_002: Kept as its own finding. BODY-002 was the O(|out|^2) containment filter and is fixed; fixing it did not touch this term, and this term would not have been fixed by it. The measurements overlap in corpus shape but not in mechanism.
findings.evidence_that_the_lookup_is_the_term: The mechanism is visible in the code rather than inferred: `for (const env of documentReferences)` runs once per span, and then the widening loop runs `for (const env of documentReferences)` again inside a while. Sorted-and-disjoint output is now established, so at most ONE envelope can contain any span, which makes the second loop provably dead and the first one a single-candidate test.
findings.proposed_fix: Binary search for the last envelope with env.start <= span.start, then test only that candidate for env.end >= span.end and strict containment. No 'find narrowest, then widen to outermost' loop is needed, because disjointness means at most one envelope can contain a span. Acceptance: an exact differential of envelopeFor against the current implementation over spans before a ref, after a ref, exactly equal bounds, strictly inside, crossing either edge, between siblings, and inside nested-looking source text with a failed outer and successful inner.
findings.not_yet_implemented: Measurement only, per the instruction to prove a real problem before optimising. The problem is now proven; the fix is the next step.

binary_search_change.what_changed: The per-span envelope lookup now uses an upper-bound binary search for the last envelope starting at or before the span, plus an explicit scan of the run of envelopes sharing span.start, instead of two full linear scans (the second of which was provably dead under the disjointness invariant).
binary_search_change.result: NEARLY NO PERFECT IMPROVEMENT: 16000 refs x 16000 spans went 8785.8ms -> 8042.4ms, about 8%, and us/row still rises 68 -> 74 -> 108 -> 169 -> 243 -> 503. The cost is NOT the lookup.
binary_search_change.why_it_is_kept: It is semantically equivalent for every input production can produce, it is strictly better asymptotically, and it removes a provably dead loop. But it must NOT be recorded as fixing this finding.
binary_search_change.semantic_gap_found_and_handled: The differential surfaced a real edge case the first version got wrong. Adjacent envelopes SHARE A BOUNDARY in production -- `${a}${b}` yields [0,4] and [4,8] -- so a span starting exactly on such a boundary is contained in the envelope that ENDS there, not only in the one that begins there, and the old rule took the NARROWER. Checking only the entry beginning at span.start picked the wider one. The lookup now considers both. The only inputs that still distinguish the two implementations are ZERO-WIDTH spans, which were not observed anywhere: across 20000 random strings plus targeted corpora, 0 of the spans found had start === end.

revised_attribution.m_2000: refs+secrets 186.6ms ; refs only 11.8ms ; secrets only 175.1ms ; neither 4.5ms
revised_attribution.conclusion: The reference machinery is about 3% of the cost. The dominant term is the SPAN side: a corpus of 8000 unique secrets with NO reference constructs at all costs 1967.9ms by itself.
revised_attribution.narrowed_further: Per-flag on 8000 unique secrets with no references: highEntropy 1528.3ms producing all 8000 spans; gitleaks 43.4ms producing 0; no detectors 13.6ms. And RedactionContext.redactText on the same text alone is 142.4ms at 2000 and 1343.1ms at 8000 -- a 4x input step giving 9.4x time. So the term is inside entropy scoring and/or the text-redaction pass, NOT the envelope lookup.

It does `spans.coverage?.attempts` and returns null when there is no attempts array, so the `attempts.find(...)` per span never executes unless coverage was collected. findings.next_step: Split refInfra into reference lookup, resolveInfraEnvelope, final remerge and applyObjectSchema; then decide the next cut. selectedOverlap is already a confirmed quadratic candidate.

containment_merge_fix.change: Pairwise-disjoint FAST PATH plus the ORIGINAL algorithm as fallback. For disjoint spans `inner` is empty by construction (containment requires overlap), so `absorbed` stays empty and `merged` is exactly `byPriority` -- the loop was spending O(n^2) to produce its own input. The disjointness check sorts by start and tests `next.start >= prev.end`, O(n log n). Overlapping or nested input falls through to the untouched original, so every attribution, inheritance and tie-break rule is unchanged.
containment_merge_fix.differential: The OLD implementation was kept as an oracle and both were instrumented to expose `byPriority`, `merged`, `emitted` and `absorbed.size`. Compared as EXACT ARRAYS over start/end/type/priority/providerType/absorbed/evidence/pathSegments/pathConfidence/indent/key/syntax/schemaEncoding AND ORDER. 10 targeted shapes (disjoint-many, nested, crossing overlap, same bounds, provider-inside-binding, entropy-inside-gitleaks, mixed priorities, adjacent-touching, single, empty) plus 30000 seeded random documents: 30010 checked, 0 differences.
containment_merge_fix.remaining_terms_at_m8000: selectedOverlap 465.7ms and refInfra 442.4ms now dominate; consolidate 131.5ms is linear.

findings.correction_of_my_inference: CORRECTED: I previously wrote that the 22% in `refInfra` must be infra recognition because the corpus has zero reference constructs. That inference was wrong to make from the corpus alone -- the infra widening stage also ends with a final remerge, `for (const span of widened...) if (!remerged.some((x) => overlaps(span, x)))`, which is itself O(m^2) at worker.js:3000. It was not listed separately in my stage table, so its cost was folded into refInfra. The next round must split refInfra into reference lookup / resolveInfraEnvelope / final remerge / applyObjectSchema before concluding anything about infra recognition.

timing_assertions_in_the_ordinary_suite_.observation: test/r3-span-density.perf.test.js failed once in a full `node --test` run and passed every time in isolation (3/3), then passed on a full re-run (434/434). The assertions in it are RATIO-based with a tail threshold, which is the right design, but `node --test` runs files in PARALLEL, so a timing ratio measured while other files are also running is not the same quantity as one measured alone.
timing_assertions_in_the_ordinary_suite_.not_a_regression: The failure could not be reproduced in three isolated runs or in a full re-run, and the corpus in question is unrelated to the change under test (a corpus record was added; no production code changed in that commit).
timing_assertions_in_the_ordinary_suite_.guidance: Treat a single timing-assertion failure in a parallel run as a FLAKE until it reproduces in isolation. Do not loosen the threshold to make it pass, and do not treat it as evidence of a regression: re-run the file alone first. The heavy sweeps belong in `npm run perf*`, which run one case per process by design.
